bullets: How to read pie charts, line graphs and bar charts, and how to compare data safely
slides.heading: Data graphs: pie charts and line graphs
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we read a pie chart of 12 pupils, follow a line graph of plants sold from January to April, compare bars for soccer and badminton, and learn why a steeper line is not always a bigger increase.

bullets: Read a pie chart: apples are 1/2 of 12 pupils, bananas and grapes are 1/4 each
Read a line graph: plants sold were Jan 20, Feb 35, Mar 30, Apr 50
Compare two bars by subtracting: 13 - 8 = 5 more chose soccer
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the three goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things.

bullets: Two shops both rose from 20 to 40, but one line looks much steeper
Does the steeper line mean a bigger increase, or is the axis tricking us?
slides.heading: Which graph is telling the truth?
slides.notes: Show the two shop graphs from scene s4 without the axis labels first: ask for a show of hands on which rose faster, take two or three answers without judging them, and say scene s4 settles this exactly.

bullets: A pie chart shows fractions of a whole: the whole class is 12 pupils
A line or bar graph has an axis scale: read the numbers before the shape
slides.heading: Every graph has parts to read first
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: first find what the whole is or what the axis counts in, then read the wedges, line or bars.

bullets: 6 of 12 pupils chose apples: the apple wedge is 1/2 of the pie
3 chose bananas and 3 chose grapes: each wedge is 1/4
slides.heading: Reading a pie chart: who likes what?
slides.notes: Narrate the twelve pupils gathering, then the wedges sweeping out: apples take half the circle, and bananas and grapes take a quarter each.

bullets: Plants sold: Jan 20, Feb 35, Mar 30, Apr 50
The line dips in March, then climbs to April: sales are rising overall
slides.heading: Reading a line graph: a rising trend
slides.notes: Follow the probe dot month to month as it draws the line: point out the small dip in March, then the climb to 50 in April.

bullets: Soccer bar: 13 votes, badminton bar: 8 votes, swimming bar: 3 votes
Read the heights, then subtract: 13 - 8 = 5
slides.heading: Worked example: comparing two bars of data
slides.notes: Watch the bars grow from the baseline, read the labels aloud, then follow the red chip as it travels the gap between the two bar tops.

bullets: Shop A and shop B both rose from 20 to 40: the same rise of +20
Graph A uses an axis of 0 to 50 and graph B uses 0 to 200, so B only looks flatter
slides.heading: Watch out: a steeper line is not always bigger
slides.notes: Hold the two graphs side by side and read the axes aloud before the lines: the same rise can look steep or flat depending on the scale.

bullets: Soccer: 13 votes, badminton: 8 votes
13 - 8 = 5 more chose soccer
slides.heading: Worked example: how many more chose soccer?
slides.notes: Talk through the bar working slowly as in scene s3 and name each step: read both heights first, then subtract the smaller from the bigger.

bullets: What fraction of the class chose bananas in the pie chart?
How many plants were sold in April, and in which month did sales dip?
slides.heading: Your turn: read, follow and compare
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them on the whole of 12 for the fraction, and on reading the axis values for the line graph.

bullets: On your own: read values from a pie chart and a line graph
Explain in one sentence why a steeper line is not always a bigger increase
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for axis values in your working, plus one clear sentence about axis scale in your explanation.
